candidates.label: Cappadocia (Roman province, label point)
candidates.support: Cappadocia's identity as the Roman province in eastern Asia Minor is undisputed. The label point is Wikidata's point for the province; Pleiades' independent 'Cappadocia (region)' entry lies about 90 km to the east, a reasonable margin for a large province label.

summary.text: Cappadocia was a Roman province in eastern Asia Minor, a kingdom until Rome annexed it in AD 17. Acts lists visitors 'from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia' at Pentecost, and the letter 1 Peter is addressed to those 'living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.'

history.text: The Roman historian Tacitus records that King Archelaus had ruled Cappadocia for fifty years when Tiberius, whom he had offended, lured him to Rome. The kingdom was then made a province under the governor Quintus Veranius, and some of the royal taxes were lowered so that Roman rule would seem mild. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates the annexation to AD 17.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Cappadocia (ruler: Quintus Veranius, sent to organize the province; then equestrian governors)
politicalHistory.note: Tacitus calls Veranius the province's "governor," though a translator's note calls his appointment "only a temporary expedient"; he later appears on the staff of Germanicus, a Roman prince. Livius likewise describes equestrian governors (procurators) for this span. This area's drawn extent also covers Pontus Galaticus (part of the province of Galatia from 2 BC, ISBE "Galatia"), Polemon's kingdom of Pontus (a client kingdom until 63, ISBE "Pontus", or 64, ISBE "Galatia", when it too joined Galatia), and Lesser Armenia (held by Archelaus of Cappadocia from 20 BC, Cassius Dio 54.9.2; by Cotys from 38, Dio 59.12.2; by Aristobulus from 54, Antiquities 20.8.4; annexed in 72, World History Encyclopedia's "Vespasian"); none of these three lands is its own area on this map, so they are not shown separately as unclear. This does not change Cappadocia's own holder; see the AD 6, AD 39 and AD 67 stops for their own changes.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Cappadocia (ruler: Gnaeus Pompeius Collega, the first governor of senatorial rank (AD 69))
politicalHistory.note: The Roman biographer Suetonius records that the emperor Vespasian "gave [Cappadocia] a consular governor in place of a Roman knight." Cappadocia and Galatia may have shared one governor from about this time on, which one modern history of the province calls likely, but no ancient source states a merger outright, so the map keeps Cappadocia and Galatia as two areas with their own holders.
